$comment: The catalog of plugins cxagent knows about. One entry per plugin; the ones cxagent itself
releases also have a directory beside this file.
MACHINE-READABLE ON PURPOSE. The plugin manager (F2, /plugin browse) and /plugin get read the
published copy of this file to show what is available and where to get it, so neither parses a
README or hardcodes a list. Keep it truthful by hand: an entry naming an asset no release carries
is worse than no entry at all. PluginCatalogTests checks each entry against the plugin's sidecar.
TWO SOURCE SHAPES. A first-party plugin says { "kind": "release", "latest": "..." } and
is fetched from cxagent's own release; anything else says { "kind": "url", "url": "..." }
and names where it actually lives. For a plugin hosted elsewhere the fields below stop being a
formality: nobody needs telling who wrote a plugin that ships beside the binary, and everybody
needs telling for one that does not. A worked entry for each shape is in cxagent.Core/sdk/docs/publishing.md.
WHAT THE HASH IS AND IS NOT. `sha256` is over the downloaded zip, and the installer refuses a
download that does not match it, or an entry that has none. It proves the bytes arrived
unaltered; it says nothing about who wrote them — that is `publisher` and `repository`, claims a
reader judges, not facts a client can verify. The separate hash the load prompt shows is over the
INSTALLED files, and answers a different question: has anything changed since you approved it.
WHERE IT COMES FROM. A `release` entry is committed with sha256 null, and the site build stamps
the hash of the zip the release actually carries into the published copy — refusing to publish
without it. A `url` entry carries its own sha256, committed by whoever adds it: it pins an exact
file somewhere this project does not control, so the hash is the only thing vouching for it, and
the site build never overwrites it. `checksums` names the release's own SHA256SUMS asset, kept for
anyone checking a download by hand; no client reads it.
PLATFORMS. A managed plugin is portable MSIL: one build runs everywhere cxagent does, so it says
`platforms: ["any"]` and has a single `source`. An ABI plugin is a native library and is NOT
portable — a .so does not load on Windows, and a publisher may ship linux-x64 and nothing else.
So an ABI entry lists the RIDs it actually has and keys its downloads by the same names:
`sources: { "linux-x64": { "kind": ..., "url" or "latest": ..., "sha256": ... } }` in
place of one `source`, each build with its own hash. The installer takes this machine's build
and, finding none, says the plugin is not available here — a better answer than downloading a
library that cannot load. RIDs are .NET's own (linux-x64, linux-arm64, osx-x64, osx-arm64,
win-x64, win-arm64), the same vocabulary the release matrix uses; `platforms` and the keys of
`sources` must agree.
A managed plugin that carries native libraries is not portable either, and uses `sources` the
same way. A first-party per-platform source is `{ "kind": "release", "latest": ...,
"sha256": null }`, like a single release source, and the site build stamps each platform's hash.
WHICH VERSION A CLIENT GETS. A `release` source uses `latest` — GitHub's always-current alias,
which resolves to the newest release carrying that asset. There is deliberately no way to ask
for a specific release's copy: every release carries the plugin (an unchanged one is re-uploaded
byte for byte), and the plugin's version tracks the plugin rather than the release. A version
this cxagent cannot load is listed with its reason and cannot be installed or updated to.

plugins.name: csharp-lsp
plugins.description: Go-to-definition, find-references and diagnostics for C#, backed by a language server. Crosses project boundaries: a reference in a test project resolves into the project under test.

requires.description: A C# language server on PATH. csharp-ls is the default and needs no configuration.

settings.server: The language server command. Defaults to csharp-ls.
settings.args: Arguments for it. OmniSharp needs ["-lsp"]; csharp-ls needs none, or ["--features","razor-support"] to analyse .razor and .cshtml.

plugins.name: calculator
plugins.description: Arithmetic a model can trust. One tool takes a whole expression and returns the exact result — a language model approximates arithmetic rather than computing it, and a calculation spread over several turns goes wrong somewhere in the middle.

plugins.name: triggers
plugins.description: Work that starts without anybody typing — on a clock. Schedules a prompt to arrive later in the same session; fires only while cxagent is running.

plugins.name: clone-finder
plugins.description: Duplicated code found without reading the repository. One tool returns the duplicated blocks ranked by size, each as locations plus a couple of lines to recognise it by — so finding duplication costs a call rather than the context the refactor then needs.

plugins.name: repo-map
plugins.description: A map of a codebase for a model that has not read it. One tool returns the most-used files' declarations — types, functions, methods, each with its line number — ranked by how much the rest of the code uses them and cut to a token budget. No language server: a dozen languages are read as text.

plugins.name: worktree
plugins.description: Sandboxes for work that should not land until someone says so. Creates a git worktree inside your folder for a sub-agent to work in, shows its diff, and merges it into your branch or throws it away — merge and discard ask first, and a merge that conflicts is undone.

requires.description: git on PATH, or its path as the git setting.

settings.folder: The folder inside yours that worktrees are made in. Defaults to .worktrees.
settings.branchPrefix: Put in front of a worktree's name to make its branch. Defaults to worktree/.
settings.git: The git command. Defaults to git.
